messages.subject: Reanalyzing the classes in a data frame
messages.subject_clean: Reanalyzing the classes in a data frame
messages.body_plain:
Hi R experts and enthusiasts. After I use subset() on a data frame to
exclude rows that have text (like "NA") in an otherwise numeric
column, the class for the now completely numeric column still remains
"factor" when I view the classes with str(). I know I can use
as.numeric() to coerce the class to numeric after I've removed the
text with subset(), but that can be time-consuming when I have several-
to-many columns to manually reclassify. So my question is: Is there a
way to have the class of all columns reanalyzed before running a
linear regression with lm()? Thanks for your time and expertise. Earl
Brown

messages.subject_clean: [StatForLing with R] Reanalyzing the classes in a data frame
messages.body_plain:
Like this?

# generate a data frame
x <- c("a", 1, 2, "b")
y <- c(0, 1, 2, "b")
z <- c("a", 1, 2, 3)
a <- data.frame(x, y, z); str(a)

# subset with [] so that only numbers remain
b <- a[2:3,]
str(b) # still factors

# reclassify
b[] <- apply(b, 2, as.numeric)

# check the result
str(b) # done

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries

messages.subject: another logistic regression with Design question
messages.subject_clean: another logistic regression with Design question
messages.body_plain:
I have a question about the intercept in lrm in the Design package:

In chapter 5, section 4 of Stephan's Statistics for Linguists with R,
model.lrm is used with a binary dependent variable (CONSTRUCTION1), a
binary independent variable (V_CHANGPOSS), and two scaled independent
variables (REC_ACT and PAT_ACT).  In the results, the Intercept
represents the default level of the V_CHANGPOSS factor
(V_CHANGPOSS=change) and the next line lists the other level of the
same factor, V_CHANGPOSS=no_change.

So far, so good - my question is how to interpret the results when
there is more than one categorical independent variable, or when the
categorical independent variables have more than two levels.

For example: a model with a binary dependent variable (Voice) with two
levels (Passive, Active), and three independent variables. One
variable (Len) is scalar; the other two are categorical: Ani, 4 levels
and Def, with 6 levels.

This produces the following output:
Intercept	-1.51968	0.32333	-4.7	0
Ani=b	-0.51932	0.30098	-1.73	0.0845
Ani=b	-0.4329	0.29655	-1.46	0.1444
Ani=b	-1.29995	0.34235	-3.8	0.0001
Def=b	-0.20174	0.13611	-1.48	0.1383
Def=c	0.12944	0.12299	1.05	0.2926
Def=d	-0.06962	1.06212	-0.07	0.9477
Def=e	-0.93456	0.52972	-1.76	0.0777
Def=f 	-0.40812	0.18146	-2.25	0.0245
Len   	-0.0393	0.02588	-1.52	0.1288

It looks like the Intercept is a combination of the first level of Ani
and the first level of Def. Is there a way to do this analysis without
an intercept?

Thanks for you help!
~Linnea

messages.subject_clean: [StatForLing with R] another logistic regression with Design question
messages.body_plain:
This can best be answered with code:

# set up
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
library(Design)
logit<-function(x) { log(x/(1-x)) }
ilogit<-function(x) { 1/(1+exp(-x)) }

# generate random data
set.seed(3)
x1 <- factor(sample(letters[1:3], 500, replace=TRUE))
x2 <- factor(sample(letters[4:6], 500, replace=TRUE))
x3 <- factor(sample(letters[8:10], 500, replace=TRUE))
y <-factor(sample(letters[25:26], 500, replace=TRUE))

# fit a model
m1 <- lrm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3)

# inspect predictions
ilogit(coef(m1)) # inverse logit of the intercept =
tapply(predict(m1, type="fitted.ind"), list(x1, x2, x3), mean)[1,1,1]
# the predicted probability when all independent vars are at their
first level

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries

University of California, Santa Barbara

messages.subject: Interaction between variables
messages.body_plain:
R and statistics experts,

I need some help interpreting the results of a logistic regression.

I was told that one way to look for interaction among variables was to
collapse two variables into one. So, I've collapse preceding
phonological context (2 variants -- high vowel, non-high vowel) with
word position (3 variants -- initial, medial, final) into a new
variable (with 6 variants). I did the same for following phonological
context and stress, each combined with word position. (This cannot be
done with scalar variables, like frequency, right? How can interaction
be tested in scalar variables?) I ran a stepwise logistic regression
(step(glm(dependent~1), dependent~ind1+ind2+ind3...)) with the newly
formed, collapsed variables as well as the original ones. So, my
question for you is:

What should I understand if one of the newly collapsed variables is
selected but the original two variables that make up the new variable
were not selected? And, what does it mean when one of the original
variables is selected but the new, collapsed variable is not?

Thank you for your time and expertise. Earl Brown

messages.subject: Re: Interaction between variables
messages.body_plain:
> I was told that one way to look for interaction among variables was to collapse two variables into one.

Uh, who told you that?? What's supposed to be the advantage of that
over the 'usual' way?

> (This cannot be done with scalar variables, like frequency, right? How can interaction be tested in scalar variables?)

Just as usual, where, by default, the interactions corresponds to the
product of the numeric variables, cf. SFLWR: 267.

STG
--
